compression.title: International Dada Archive
compression.lede: is the University of Iowa Libraries' archive of the historic Dada movement, founded in 1979, with a catalog of about 60,000 titles and a Digital Dada Library of page scans (home page); its Books by Author list holds a pen name beside a civil name, one book under both, with no stated rule (census record).

sentences.text: The International Dada Archive, at the University of Iowa Libraries in Iowa City, was founded in 1979 and describes itself as "a scholarly resource for the study of the historic Dada movement" that "has compiled a comprehensive collection of documentation and scholarship relating to Dada".

Its collection is made up of works by and about the dadaists, in books, articles, microfilmed manuscript collections, video and sound recordings and online resources, and it focuses its collection and study on a named list of individuals.

An earlier form of the front page, quoted by International Times in 2019, gave the founding "as part of the Dada Archive and Research Center", a parent body the front page read on 1 November 2026 does not name.

A 2017 article in The Gazette traces the collection to an international conference on Dada that the university hosted in 1978, "during which scholars discussed the need to collect and preserve work related to the movement", after which the library's Special Collections department "became the place for that repository".

The curator, Timothy Shipe, has worked with the collection since 1980, and his history of the Archive answers the question "Why Iowa?" with "a clear affinity between the Dada movement and this University".

The manuscript microfilms were made in public and private collections in Europe and North America in the early 1980s, with funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities and the Jerome Foundation, and each microfilmed collection has a detailed finding aid.

The collection is housed in various departments of the University of Iowa Libraries, most of it in the Main Library or the Art Library and the original Dada-era publications in the Special Collections Department, at 100 Main Library, Iowa City.
The same 2017 article says the University "now holds one of the world's largest Dada collections"; the Capture Registry finds the rank on no page the census saved.

Primary access to the whole collection is through the International Online Bibliography of Dada, "a catalog containing approximately 60,000 titles" in all formats catalogued for it, from books and essays in books to periodical articles, manuscripts and sound and video recordings; the figure is undated in the source.

The Digital Dada Library gives scanned images of original Dada-era publications in two sections, periodicals of the movement from Zurich, Berlin, Paris and elsewhere, and books by participants with ephemera such as exhibition catalogs and broadsides.

The periodicals run from 291 and 391 to Zenit and Der Zweemann, thirty-six titles as International Times counted them in 2019 and as the census counted them from the saved list in 2026; the Archive states no count.
Each original is scanned whole as page images, "not searchable full-text files", and the pages can be downloaded.

Many runs are incomplete: the Library generally includes only originals held in Special Collections, though the Archive owns complete reprints of most of the periodicals, and the few reprints it does include omit copyrighted matter such as new prefaces and critical annotations.

The Archive publishes Dada/Surrealism, a peer-reviewed, open-access electronic journal sponsored by the Association for the Study of Dada and Surrealism, which the 2017 article gives as published by the University.
The census holds the journal apart from the collection: the Archive publishes Dada/Surrealism, and its collection focuses on the historic Dada movement.
Scholars may visit by appointment, those from out of town well in advance, since access to some resources is limited when the curator is away, and enquiries go to the curator.
The scans are "provided for research purposes only", and no licence is stated.

The Archive has no staff for interlibrary loan; a requester's library is to treat it as a "lender of last resort" and as a special collection within the Libraries, and unpublished manuscript material cannot normally be loaned.

In the 2017 article the curator reads Dada as having "gradually crystallized into essentially an anti-war movement", on the occasion of an exhibit, Documenting Dada/Disseminating Dada, in the Main Library gallery.

The Digital Dada Library files its books by author, and its headings, with those of its list of dadaists, carry a second name in parentheses where one is given, in either order: "SALOMO FRIEDLAENDER (MYNONA)", "Iliazd (Ilia Zdanevich)", "JEAN (HANS) ARP", and three names in "EDGAR FIRN (KARL DÖHMAN) (DAIMONIDES)".
One book, ZIEK; EENE MOEDER; HERTETOLKEN, stands under "JULIUS KREKEL (CLÉMENT PANSAERS)" and again under "CLÉMENT PANSAERS".
The two lists give some names differently: "JEAN ARP" in the one and "JEAN (HANS) ARP" in the other, "(DAIMONIDES)" and "(DIAMONIDES)", "Iliazd (Ilia Zdanevich)" and "ILIAZD".
Wikipedia's article on Dada uses the double form, "Iliazd (Ilia Zdanevich)", and cites the Archive's page on him.

No naming policy is stated in the saved pages: the census records the authorial function as "not stated as a rule", which name carries a work "left undecided", and responsibility for the holdings with the Libraries and the curator.

The census reads the list as historical lineage for its question of how authorship is named and held: "a pen name and a civil name stand side by side and one book is held under both, so the chosen name survives as a heading and no reduction to one name is performed".

Reduction is the term of #940, where "modern attribution regimes concentrate authority by collapsing distinct authorial functions into one legally legible identity", the civil name serving as "the atomic unit of attribution", and reduction is "the claim that the civil bearer exhausts the authorial function".

#940 separates the pseudonym, "a different name for a work whose authorial function is nonetheless traceable to the civil identity that stands behind the name", from the heteronym by markers it calls testable: "A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself."

Other deposits define the pseudonym by concealment, "A pseudonym conceals identity" (#1127) and pseudonymy "where the author conceals identity" beside the pen name "where the author adopts a label" (#794), and the archive's typology of authorial voices (#667) gives a pseudonym as "a name substitution", the writing remaining "that of the biographical person".

The typology notes that these terms are "sometimes used interchangeably in critical writing, and sometimes with sharp distinction", and holds that the distinctions "correspond to genuinely different literary operations".

On the census's reading the list leaves the question open: "No rule in the saved sources says which name governs, and the list does not show whether any of these names constitutes a distinct authorial function in #940's sense", and which name the Archive treats as the author's own is among what it does not answer.
#1722 asks that an answer name "the object at its own level: a person, a pen name, a paper, an institute, an event", each existing "in their own way" with "its own kind of evidence".

The Libraries' page for the Archive is its "gateway to the International Online Bibliography of Dada" and states that "As the site is developed" it will add information on the movement and its writers and artists; the About page of the Archive's site, as saved on 1 November 2026, holds the navigation and a template placeholder, "This is an example page."
The site links other Dada resources and archives, among them the Arp Museum, the Bauhaus Archive and the Kurt Schwitters Archive.
Wikipedia has no article under the name; its article on Dada lists the Archive among its external links as "early Dada periodicals, online scans of publications".

The People's Graphic Design Archive listed it on 26 December 2023, added by Louise Sandhaus, with the front page's opening text and the tags Dada, publication, magazine, European Design, Journals, archive and Modernism; International Times carried in 2019 Colin Marshall's Open Culture post on the Digital Dada Library, which asks where one would look for Dada publications and suggests the University of Iowa.

Asked for the Archive by its name on 1 November 2026, a new address, Google's AI Overview, signed out, composed it from four cards, and the Capture Registry reads the composition as "Faithful to the archive's own page on founding, holdings and count, with a conference, a world rank and a co-publisher on no saved page".
The conference and the rank stand in The Gazette's article of 2017, the composition's third card.

The Registry records the composition's "Co-publisher" against the page's "published by the International Dada Archive", the terms of use and the curator left out, and the Books by Author with its double names not carried: the composition "gives no account of how the list files a writer".

O940-01.quote: modern attribution regimes concentrate authority by collapsing distinct authorial functions into one legally legible identity
O940-01.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

O940-02.quote: A civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern legitimacy in scholarly, literary, institutional, and platform-mediated production.
O940-02.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

O940-06.quote: What heteronymy refuses is not attribution. It is *reduction* — the claim that the civil bearer exhausts the authorial function
O940-06.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

O940-03.quote: Pseudonymy is using a different name for a work whose authorial function is nonetheless traceable to the civil identity that stands behind the name.
O940-03.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

O940-04.quote: A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself.
O940-04.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

O940-05.quote: These are testable. A pseudonymic operation would fail one or more (typically the disagreement, the position, or the substrate-declaration criteria).
O940-05.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

O1127-01.quote: A heteronym is not a pseudonym. A pseudonym conceals identity. A heteronym creates it.
O1127-01.source_label: #1127 Constitution of the Semantic Economy — Enacted Version 1.0

O794-01.quote: distinct from pseudonymy (where the author conceals identity) and from simple pen names (where the author adopts a label)
O794-01.source_label: #794 Mary Lee Is a Heteronym: On Institutional Authorship, Entity Substitution, and the Composition Layer's Preference for the More Confabulated Name

O667-02.quote: A pseudonym is a name substitution: an author publishes under a different name for reasons of privacy, commercial convenience, or social protection, while the writing remains that of the biographical person.
O667-02.source_label: #667 Heteronymic Typology A Formal Classification of Authorial Voices in Pessoa and Beyond EA-PKG-02 · v1.0

O667-01.quote: Pseudonym, pen-name, alias, nom-de-plume, stage name, authorial persona, heteronym, semi-heteronym — these terms are sometimes used interchangeably in critical writing, and sometimes with sharp distinction.
O667-01.source_label: #667 Heteronymic Typology A Formal Classification of Authorial Voices in Pessoa and Beyond EA-PKG-02 · v1.0

O667-03.quote: These are not small distinctions. They correspond to genuinely different literary operations. … The Pessoa Knowledge Graph (EA-PKG-01) depends on this typology being encoded as distinct graph categories.
O667-03.source_label: #667 Heteronymic Typology A Formal Classification of Authorial Voices in Pessoa and Beyond EA-PKG-02 · v1.0
